name: Grounds For Thought: August Lineup
description: Grounds for Thought: August 2026A Blue Tokai × unLecture SeriesFour Thursday evenings. Four very different conversations. Grounds for Thought is a monthly series where Blue Tokai and unLecture bring researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into a coffee shops. The format is simple: an expert, a room full of curious people, and a conversation that goes somewhere a classroom rarely does.6th August: Shambhavi TiwariPossessed: The Ghost, The Asylum, The Priest, and the PeopleWhen someone in rural India is "possessed by a ghost," they encounter not just their family and their priest, but eventually — often — a psychiatrist. Two completely different frameworks for what has gone wrong, and what healing looks like. This session uses spirit possession across Indian cultural contexts to examine what happens when indigenous knowledge systems and clinical medicine cross paths. PhD researcher Shambhavi Tiwari, who has spent years in this space, asks: superstition, myth, knowledge system, or something else entirely?13th August: Dr. Vishwas ChitaleZoom In, Zoom Out: What India's Climate Risk Looks Like at Ground LevelEveryone has heard the national climate numbers. But zoom into a district, and the picture changes entirely — neighbouring areas with opposite risk profiles, and disaster plans built on averages too coarse to catch where the real danger sits. Dr. Vishwas Chitale, Fellow at CEEW, will walk us through India's climate risk from the national level down to your own neighbourhood — and then hand the tool to the room. Participants will pull up their own hometown's actual climate risk profile live, using CRAVIS, CEEW's climate intelligence platform. You'll leave having done a small piece of the research yourself.20th August: Antara ChakrabartyFrom Village to Viral: How Folk Music Got a Second LifeA seventeenth-century Sufi verse now has a hundred million YouTube views. The songs of Lalon Fakir, Bengal's wandering poet-saint, are uniting two Bengals and two centuries through a single melody. This session traces folk music's remarkable journey — from Punjab's Sufi shrines and Bengal's riverside Baul gatherings to studio stages and streaming platforms — and asks the questions nobody quite wants to answer. Who owns a folk song? What happens when heritage becomes entertainment? Does something get lost in translation, or does it simply learn a new way to survive? Expect live music, a few surprises, and a fresh way of listening to songs you may already love.27th August: Sunaina SaxenaWhat is a Clean Street Worth?Why are two seemingly identical houses priced so differently? This session explores one of environmental economics' most elegant tools, hedonic pricing, to answer a question most of us have never thought to ask: does the cleanliness of a neighbourhood have a measurable economic value? Through stories, discussion, and simple examples, researcher Sunaina Saxena explores how clean streets, reliable waste collection, and a healthy living environment become embedded in housing prices — and what that reveals about our cities and the choices we make about where we live.

name: The Making of a Serial Offender
description: Join us for an evening that begins with a simple question: what does a serial offender look like? The answer may be more unsettling than you think.About the LectureThe point is not that everyone is a criminal. The point is that none of us can recognise one by looking.This lecture explores how criminal profiling moved beyond outdated assumptions about "criminal faces" to become one of the most fascinating tools in modern investigations. Drawing from forensic psychology, criminology, and real-world case studies, the session examines how investigators attempt to understand offenders through behaviour rather than appearance.Together, we'll explore:Why humans are often poor judges of who is capable of violenceThe evolution of criminal profiling, from early theories to modern investigative psychologyHow crime scene behaviour can reveal patterns of motive, planning, control, and escalationThe origins of behavioural profiling and the rise of the FBI's Behavioural Science UnitWhat famous serial offender cases reveal about fantasy, victim selection, and criminal developmentWhy serial offending remains understudied in IndiaHow forensic psychologists and investigators use Behavioural Evidence Analysis to reconstruct offender behaviourMoving beyond sensationalism and popular crime shows, this lecture examines the deeper psychological and social questions that profiling raises. Why do some individuals cross lines that most never do? What can behaviour tell us about risk, intent, and future offending? And how can India build more rigorous behavioural science frameworks for criminal investigation?Part psychology, part criminology, and part investigative science, this session offers a rare glimpse into the complex process of understanding criminal behaviour.About the SpeakerMr. Rithin Joseph is an Assistant Professor at the School of Behavioural Forensics, National Forensic Sciences University (NFSU), Delhi. Specialising in Criminology and Forensic Psychology, his work focuses on criminal profiling, deception detection, investigative psychology, and forensic behavioural analysis. He has published multiple research papers and presented over twenty-one papers at national and international conferences.Mr. Joseph has specialised training in a range of forensic investigative techniques, including Polygraph, Brain Electrical Oscillation Signature Profiling (BEOS), Suspect Detection System (SDS), Layered Voice Analysis (LVA), and EyeDetect. He currently serves as Co-Investigator on an ICSSR-funded research project examining the prediction of recidivism among first-time offenders in conflict with the law. He is also the co-author of "Crime as the Cause of Criminality" and "BRICS: Unravelling the Abyss."A Gold Medalist in Criminology from the National Forensic Sciences University and recipient of the Young Criminologist Award 2024, he continues to contribute to research in criminal psychology, offender behaviour, and investigative science while mentoring postgraduate students and pursuing doctoral research in Criminal Psychology.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. Created by three friends from college who wanted learning to feel warm, social and alive — unLecture turns an otherwise ordinary evening into a conversation you may think about long after it ends.

name: India's Youth: Jobs, Aspirations & Possibilities
description: Join us for a lecture about a number that should be reshaping how we think about India's future:The population of Indian students aged 15 and above doubled in two decades, from 60 million in 2004-05 to 120 million in 2023-24.About the LectureThose numbers above signal a staggering rise in aspiration for upward mobility among young Indians, despite the social disadvantages many of them face. It also means India has the potential to propel itself to the forefront of the knowledge economy — if the quality of education improves at every level.But there's a harder truth underneath the aspiration: research shows slow growth of regular, decent jobs in India, especially in manufacturing and high-value services. Not only are the country's long-term growth prospects at risk, but historically entrenched inequalities could get reinforced in the labour market rather than dissolved by it.This lecture makes the case that India's future growth will have to be built much more on incomes generated within the country than on export demand from abroad, a virtuous cycle of more jobs, higher incomes, and greater domestic demand.The session explores:Why the doubling of India's student population is both an opportunity and a warning signWhat the data shows about the slow growth of decent jobs in manufacturing and high-value servicesHow historically determined inequalities risk being reinforced, rather than resolved, in the labour marketWhy domestic demand, not exports may be the key to India's next phase of growthAbout the SpeakerJayan Jose Thomas is a Professor of Economics at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi, where he has taught since July 2010. He has also served as a Member of the State Planning Board, Government of Kerala. His research addresses development problems related to labour and industrialisation from a macroeconomic perspective, spanning the Indian economy, international development and macroeconomic theory. He previously held a four-year academic position at the National University of Singapore. His research has appeared in journals including World Development, Development and Change, and Economic and Political Weekly, and he contributes regularly to The Hindu.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. description: Join us for a lecture that challenges one of our most protected assumptions: Are children always innocent? A Gold Medallist in Criminology with a specialisation in Human Rights, she brings a background in Media and Communication to her research. name: Forwarded as Received: Misinformation 101
description: Join us for a lecture that asks a question with no comfortable answer:If the people deciding what counts as true are working from the same broken information as everyone else, who do we trust to hold the line?About The Lecture"Fake news" was always too small a phrase. It suggested a fabricated story, a fact-check, a correction — a problem that could, in theory, be solved. What we're actually living through is something else: real photographs stripped of context, selective truths, political insinuation, and claims repeated in enough WhatsApp groups until they stop needing to be true at all.Drawing on her book "Forwarded as Received: How Misinformation Turns Viral, Violent and True," this lecture looks past the individual act of falling for a hoax and toward the larger machinery — how misinformation and malinformation move through digital platforms, political campaigns, and even bureaucratic institutions, shaping not just what people believe, but who gets counted, trusted, or excluded.This isn't a lecture about how other people get fooled. It's about how the very systems built to establish "the facts" — platforms, institutions, public systems — can become vulnerable to the same distortions they claim to correct.About the SpeakerSaadia Azim is the author of "Forwarded as Received: How Misinformation Turns Viral, Violent and True" (Simon & Schuster India), which examines how misinformation moves through everyday social behaviour, politics, media and technology to acquire the force of public truth. She is Chief Operating Officer of the Government of West Bengal's Digital Public Service Delivery Programme, a former journalist, and an Internet Society Mid-Career Fellow. Her work focuses on misinformation, digital governance, algorithmic power, public trust and democratic behaviour in India and the Global South.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. name: Decoding The Unspoken Through Body Language
description: Join us for a lecture that might make you rethink every conversation you've ever had.About the LectureA raised eyebrow. A shift in posture. A half-second pause before an answer. Long before you finish a sentence, your body has usually already told the room the truth.This lecture explores body language as one of the most powerful, and most overlooked, forms of communication we have.
